title: Why Anthropic Reported a $104 Billion Net Loss

sources.locator: Summary Consolidated Financial and Other Data, p. 27; MD&A, Change in Fair Value of Convertible Notes, Derivative Liabilities, and SAFEs; Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows, nine months ended September 30, 2026
sources.note: Issuer's preliminary prospectus filed on EDGAR. Figures are USD millions for the unaudited nine months ended September 30, 2026.

claims.text: For the nine months ended September 30, 2026, consolidated operating loss was $1,260 million and net loss was $104,039 million.

The fair-value change for convertible notes, derivative liabilities and SAFEs was a $94,324 million charge. Anthropic attributes the increase primarily to outstanding convertible promissory notes rising in fair value as its enterprise valuation increased.
In USD millions: −1,260 operating loss + 2,359 interest income − 94,324 fair-value charge − 10,397 other net expense − 417 income tax expense = −104,039 net loss.
The cash flow statement adds back the $94,324 million fair-value charge in its reconciliation from net loss to operating cash flow. The charge itself is not a $94,324 million cash payment.
Compute and infrastructure expense was $18,808 million in the same nine months. That is an operating expense category.

A rise in enterprise valuation can increase the fair value of outstanding financing obligations and therefore worsen reported earnings. Whether growth becomes sustainable profit remains an analytical question.

scenes.title: Where did the money go?
scenes.narration: Anthropic reported a hundred-and-four-billion-dollar loss. So where did the money go?

scenes.title: Financing obligations
scenes.narration: Some of its financing obligations rise in value with the company.

scenes.title: The valuation changed
scenes.narration: Revaluing them created a ninety-four-point-three-billion-dollar charge.
labels: Fair value of outstanding notes rises

scenes.title: A charge goes into net loss
scenes.narration: That charge went into the accounts, pushing the reported nine-month loss above a hundred billion dollars. The revaluation itself involved no equivalent cash payment.
labels: No cash payment from this charge

scenes.title: Compute is still a big expense
scenes.narration: But the running costs were still enormous. Compute and infrastructure alone approached nineteen billion dollars in those same nine months.

scenes.title: Valuation, accounting and lasting profit
scenes.narration: So a rising valuation can make the accounts look worse. Whether that growth becomes sustainable profit is the question still waiting for an answer.
